subject: The Bank of Canada changed which inflation it watches
bodyMarkdown:
The Bank of Canada sets rates again on December 9, and on Tuesday it changed which inflation number it will hold up when it does. **Core inflation**, the version of the consumer price index that strips out the jumpiest prices to show the underlying trend, will now come from a different pair of gauges, and one of the old ones is being scrapped.

## What actually changed

Governor Tiff Macklem spoke at the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto on Tuesday, and CTV News and CP24 both led with the same line out of it: the Bank admitted it had sent mixed messages about core inflation in the past. The renewed framework behind the speech keeps the 2% target at the midpoint of a 1% to 3% control range, now running January 2027 through December 2031. The day to day change is in the measures. Bloomberg reported on Tuesday that the Bank will lead with CPI-trim and **CPIX**, an older gauge that excludes eight volatile items and guided Bank decisions from 2001 to 2016. CPI-common, the third of the current trio, is being discontinued for lack of use. The Bank also says it will publish a public inflation dashboard.

## The number depends on which gauge you pick

Statistics Canada's October release on November 16 put headline inflation at 3.1% year over year, flat from September. Underneath it, CPI-trim came in at 1.8%, down from 1.9%, CPI-median held at 2.0%, and CPI-common rose to 2.5% from 2.4%. So the measure being retired is the one that was moving up, and one of the two being promoted sits furthest below target. I do not think the Bank picked its gauges to flatter itself. CPI-common has been criticized for years and it gets revised, so dropping it is defensible on the merits. The effect is still real. A reader checking core inflation last week saw a spread of 1.8% to 2.5%, and from Tuesday the official framing starts near the bottom of that spread while the price index households actually live with sits at 3.1%.

## What Macklem conceded

CP24 quoted him saying the Bank had been "too slow to recognize the persistence of inflationary pressures and how broadly they were spreading through the economy". He was also firm that the target has not moved. "Total CPI inflation is our target, and it will be front and centre in all our communications," he said, describing the core measures as an input to the outlook rather than a target of their own. That line tells you how to read the next few months. BNN Bloomberg reported the same day that his inflation forecast has come down somewhat while oil prices keep pressure on how long inflation lasts. The Bank raised its policy rate a quarter point to 2.50% on October 28 after roughly a year on hold, and CBC reported after the October CPI that economists expect a hold on December 9.

## The takeaway

Watch which number Macklem leads with at the December 9 press conference, because Tuesday told you he has a new default and the first use of it will set the tone. If you are renewing a mortgage in the next year, the figure that moves your payment is the policy rate at 2.50%, not whichever core gauge is in fashion, so price the renewal off the rate path rather than the commentary. The next CPI print is scheduled for December 14, which falls after the decision, so the Bank rules on October data and the rest of us find out afterward whether the new gauges were right. When the dashboard goes live, bookmark it and check CPIX against your own grocery bill.
